notes.claim: BS 7671 itself has no diversity table; Regulation 311.1 asks the designer to assess maximum demand (of the whole installation or a part of it), and the On-Site Guide gives the recognised figures.
Maximum demand is the largest current an installation draws at any one time, which is why the supply and every submain are sized from it.
Diversity is common-sense guidance from the On-Site Guide's Appendix A, not a rule; the slides give 66% for a domestic lighting circuit as the example.

Sources differ on where diversity is applied: the course slides apply 66% to the Ib of a lighting circuit, while a training provider says diversity applies to the aggregate demand at the origin, not to individual circuits.
notes.contested: Dan's slides apply diversity to the design current of a lighting circuit; Total Skills says to size each circuit on its full design current and apply diversity only to the aggregate demand.

notes.claim: The assignment asks for loads to be balanced across circuits (question 1b), links this to the maximum-demand question 10, and points to Section 3 of The Electrical Installation Guide for demand and diversity factors.
Balanced fundamental currents leave no current in the neutral (a balanced motor load needs no neutral), and an IET forum contributor suggests spreading demand about one third to each phase.
For the EV charge points the guide says load management may be considered to reduce maximum demand but is not compulsory, and Regulation 722.311 lets load curtailment be taken into account.

The lighting drawing's key gives each fitting's wattage (for example 4 × 36 W modular fluorescent, 58 W twin fluorescent, 70 W column luminaires), to be recounted by hand; the power drawing marks 63 A isolators and 2 × 32 A EV points.
